canonical_topic: Daylight saving time and Indiana electricity demand
definition: A real-world illustration of a model's underlying assumption silently reversing as the environment around it changed.
core_idea: A mid-1970s study found that shifting clocks for daylight saving in summer slightly reduced energy use by extending evening daylight; when Indiana finally adopted daylight saving roughly thirty years later, the state instead saw a noticeable increase in power consumption, which was attributed to air conditioning — largely absent in the 1970s — having since become the dominant summer electricity use, so extra evening daylight now drove more cooling demand instead of less lighting demand.
key_points: 1970s study concluded daylight saving time modestly cut energy use, at a time when lighting was the dominant driver of summer electricity use
About thirty years later, Indiana's actual switch to daylight saving produced a measurable increase in power consumption instead
The reversal is attributed to the intervening widespread adoption of air conditioning, which shifted the dominant driver of electricity demand from lighting to cooling
The case shows a model's real-world conclusion can flip sign entirely as the underlying drivers of the system change, with no error in the original analysis itself
relationships: Illustrates assumption risk from long model lifespans
